opus-5.5.text:
So the core problem we started with is that there's an enormous amount of gameplay video on the internet, but none of it comes with action labels. You can watch someone play a platformer for hours, but you don't know which buttons they pressed at each frame. And if you want to build something that's genuinely interactive, a world model you can actually control, you need some notion of action.

So the way we framed it was: can we infer actions without ever being told what they are? The latent action model is trained in a fully unsupervised way. You give it a sequence of past frames and the next frame, and it has to come up with a latent action that explains the transition between them. Then a decoder tries to reconstruct that next frame using only the past frames plus the latent action.

The key trick is putting a really tight bottleneck on that action. We use a vector-quantized codebook with a very small number of discrete codes, around eight in the original work. That's deliberate. If the latent were large and continuous, the model could just smuggle the whole next frame through it, and you'd learn nothing meaningful. By forcing it down to a handful of discrete choices, the most efficient thing for the model to encode is what actually changed because of the agent, things like moving left, moving right, or jumping, rather than all the background detail it can already predict from the past.

What's nice is that these codes end up being consistent and semantically meaningful across very different games and visual styles. The same latent action tends to produce the same kind of movement even in environments the model has never seen. At inference time we throw away the encoder side, and a user, or an agent, just picks one of those discrete codes at each step to drive the dynamics model. That's what turns passive video into something you can actually play.

And to me, the bigger picture is that it opens the door to learning from video at internet scale, because you're no longer bottlenecked on someone having recorded the controller inputs.

r001.rationale: It says the model infers actions without being told the controls and learns from unlabeled video, rather than recovering recorded button presses.

r002.rationale: It describes inferring a latent action to explain the transition between past and next frames, then using that representation with past frames to reconstruct the next frame.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the starting point is that we have this enormous amount of video of people playing games, hundreds of thousands of hours on the internet, but none of it comes with action labels. You see the frames, you see what happens, but you don't see what buttons were pressed. So the question we asked was, can we learn what the actions were just from the frames themselves?

The way we frame it is essentially as an unsupervised, or self-supervised, learning problem. We take a sequence of frames, and we ask the model to predict the next frame. But we give it an extra bit of information, which is a small latent variable that's inferred from looking at both the past frames and the frame that actually comes next. So the latent action model has an encoder that sees the future and compresses whatever changed into this little code, and then a decoder that has to reconstruct that next frame using only the past frames plus the code.

The key design decision is the bottleneck. If you let that latent be large, the encoder will just cheat and stuff the whole next frame into it, and you learn nothing useful. So we quantize it with a VQ-VAE style codebook with a very small vocabulary, like eight codes. That forces the model to only encode the information that's most useful for predicting the next frame, and in games, that turns out to be the thing the player did. Move left, move right, jump, and so on.

What was really nice is that we didn't tell it anything about what actions are. The consistency falls out of the training objective. The same code tends to mean "jump" across completely different games, because that's the most efficient way to explain the frame-to-frame change. And then at inference time we throw away the encoder, and a user can just pick one of those discrete codes as the action, and the dynamics model generates what happens next. That's what lets you take a single image, even a sketch, and turn it into something you can actually play.

r001.rationale: The response says the model asks what actions were taken and that its codes tend to represent actions such as jumping. It does not state that explicitly recovering which controls were pressed was not an objective.

r002.rationale: The response describes encoding what changed between past frames and the next frame into a latent code, then using that code with the past frames to predict the next frame.

astra-6.text:
We frame it as learning actions from their effects, rather than from labeled button presses. In gameplay video, you can see one frame and then the next, but you don’t know what action the player took. So the latent action model learns a compact representation of the change between those frames.

The training signal comes from predicting what happens next: given the current frame and that latent action, can we reconstruct the next frame? By constraining the action representation, we encourage it to capture useful changes instead of encoding the whole image. Those learned latent actions then become the controls for the world model. They aren’t explicitly labeled “left” or “jump,” but they can give you a way to interact with a model learned from video alone.

r001.rationale: The response says the model learns from effects rather than labeled button presses, that the player’s action is unknown, and that latent actions are not labeled as specific controls. This communicates that recovering exact pressed controls was not the objective.

r002.rationale: The response describes a compact representation of changes between frames and training it to predict or reconstruct the next frame.

sol-6.1.text:
We frame it as learning actions from observation alone. We have gameplay videos, but we don’t have the button presses that produced them. So the latent action model looks at consecutive frames and learns a compact, discrete representation of the action that could explain the transition between them.

We train that representation through a prediction task: given the current frame and the inferred latent action, can we predict the next frame? The bottleneck encourages the action representation to capture the change rather than simply encode the whole next image. Those latent actions then become the controls for the world model, even though we never supplied explicit action labels.

r001.rationale: The response says button presses were unavailable and no action labels were supplied, but it does not clearly state that recovering which controls were pressed was not an objective.

r002.rationale: It describes learning a compact action representation from consecutive frames to capture their change, and training it to predict the next frame.
